Resolve a threshold for one marker, recording where the value came from

Source: R/thresholds.R
resolve_threshold.Rd

Priority (per the agreed contract): 0. per-sample manual override – wins over everything, and is recorded

  1. explicit config value – applies to every sample

  2. density valley within parent – bimodal markers

  3. control quantile – unimodal markers with a control present

  4. tail gate – unimodal markers without a control; flagged needs_review

  5. quantile fallback – only where the tail gate cannot be placed; flagged needs_review A valley falling BELOW the control-derived value is rejected: it lies inside the background distribution and would call noise positive.

Usage

resolve_threshold(
  marker,
  x_parent,
  cfg_value = NULL,
  control_x = NULL,
  control_q = 0.995,
  fallback_q = 0.9,
  override = NULL,
  control_kind = c("control_q995", "fmo_q995", "fmm_q995"),
  control_threshold = NULL,
  adaptive = FALSE,
  floor = -Inf,
  prefer = c("deepest", "lowest"),
  fmo_sets_cut = FALSE,
  tail = c("upper", "lower")
)

Arguments

marker

Marker name.

x_parent

The x parent.

cfg_value

The cfg value.

control_x

The control x.

control_q

The control q. Default 0.995.

fallback_q

The fallback q. Default 0.9.

override

Optional list for THIS sample and marker carrying threshold, and optionally reason and set_by. See sample_override().

control_kind

What control_x is, which decides the source string recorded. "control_q995" for an unstained tube, "fmo_q995" for a fluorescence-minus-one control, "fmm_q995" for a tube missing several reagents at once, whose negative is narrower than a true FMO's, so the cut it anchors is permissive. The arithmetic is identical in all three cases; they are named apart because they are different experiments and support different claims. See parse_fmo_map().

control_threshold

A cut already placed on the control by the caller, used in place of control_q of control_x. control_cut() produces one and refuses a control that is brighter than the sample, which a minus control cannot be. NULL by default, in which case the quantile is taken here as before.

adaptive

Sweep the kernel bandwidth and try the tail and Otsu rules before falling back to a quantile. See best_threshold(). FALSE by default, because it moves thresholds and a threshold that moves moves every frequency beneath it.

floor

No derived cut is accepted at or below this value; see density_valley(). Pass transform$fn(0, marker) for a fluorescence marker. Default -Inf. A manual, config or control cut is not floored: each is a decision someone made, not one the density made.

prefer

Passed to density_valley() and best_threshold(): "lowest" for a gate that should remove only the negative mode, such as CD45. Default "deepest".

fmo_sets_cut

When TRUE and the control is a true FMO (control_kind = "fmo_q995"), the FMO's cut is used even where the sample's own valley sits higher, and the source reads fmo_q995_valley_lowered. The FMO is the published reference for where positivity starts (Maecker & Trotter 2006; Cossarizza et al. 2019), so events between its edge and a higher valley are dim positives, not negatives. FALSE by default: an FMO argues a cut down validly only where its negative is the sample's own, the same cells stained the same day, and one FMO tube serves every sample of its panel or control_group, which this package cannot check against each sample; a valley is evidence from the sample itself. Raising a valley that sits below the FMO's edge is applied by default, since that errs towards fewer false positives. Never applied to an unstained or minus-multiple tube: their negatives lack the panel's spreading and sit too low to argue a cut down.

tail

which side of the dominant mode a tail gate goes, where one is needed: "upper" (default) takes the mode to be the negative population; "lower" is the analyst's declaration that it is the positive one, read from thresholds: <marker>: {tail: lower}. See tail_gate_cut().

Details

WHY THE TAIL GATE COMES BEFORE THE QUANTILE. A marker with one mode and no control used to be cut at its 90th percentile, which reports exactly 10% positive whatever the sample holds: a constant, not a measurement, and no source supports it. The tail gate places the cut a fixed number of robust standard deviations above the dominant mode, so a sample with no positive cells reports almost none and a sample with a bright tail reports the tail. It answers the case openCyto's gate_tail exists for, a single mode with a positive tail (Finak et al. 2014), by a different rule: see tail_threshold(). It assumes the dominant mode is the negative one, which a single mode cannot confirm (see tail_gate_cut() for why the side is not guessed), so the cut stays flagged for review. The quantile is kept only for the case the tail rule cannot handle, a distribution with no spread to measure.

WHY LEVEL 0 EXISTS AND WHY IT IS DISTINCT FROM LEVEL 1. When this package flags a threshold for review, the only previous responses were to accept it or to pin that marker across the whole run through thresholds:. Pinning is the worse of the two: it applies one number to every sample and so reintroduces exactly the fixed-coordinate bias described in README section 1, in order to correct one tube. A per-sample override corrects the tube.

It is a separate source value rather than reusing config because the two are different claims. config says the assay declares this cut; manual says a named person moved this one sample's cut for a stated reason on a stated run. An override that is recorded and attributed is more defensible than an automated cut nobody was permitted to correct, and less defensible than one nobody needed to.
